questions.stem: In the neuron shown, what is the main function of the structure labeled D?
choices: It receives chemical messages from other neurons.
It releases neurotransmitters into the synapse.
It insulates the axon and speeds the transmission of the electrical signal.
It contains the nucleus and maintains the cell's life.
questions.explanation: D is the myelin sheath. Its segments insulate the axon, so the impulse jumps between the gaps (nodes), which is much faster than conduction along an unmyelinated axon.

questions.stem: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that gradually destroys structure D in the diagram. Which symptom pattern would be expected?
choices: Slowed and disrupted communication between the brain and muscles, leading to weakness and loss of coordination
Overproduction of neurotransmitters, leading to seizures
An inability of the neuron to receive any messages from other neurons
Faster neural transmission, leading to exaggerated reflexes
questions.explanation: Without myelin, signals travel slowly and can fail along the axon. Because motor commands are delayed or lost, multiple sclerosis typically produces weakness, numbness, and problems with coordination and vision.

questions.stem: Which labeled part of the neuron is specialized to receive messages from other neurons?
questions.explanation: A marks the dendrites, branching fibers covered in receptor sites. Messages travel from the dendrites to the cell body (B), along the axon (C), and out through the terminal buttons (E).

questions.stem: Neurotransmitter molecules are stored in vesicles and released into the synaptic gap from which labeled structure?
questions.explanation: E marks the axon terminals, or terminal buttons. When an action potential arrives, vesicles fuse with the terminal membrane and release neurotransmitters, which cross the synapse to the next neuron's dendrites.

questions.stem: The rapid rise in the segment labeled B is caused mainly by which event?
choices: Positively charged potassium ions flow out of the axon.
Positively charged sodium ions rush into the axon through opened channels.
Neurotransmitters cross the synapse into the axon.
The myelin sheath releases stored electrical charge.
questions.explanation: Once threshold is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions flood in, so the inside of the axon briefly becomes positive (depolarization). The later fall, C, occurs as potassium flows out.

questions.stem: During the segment labeled D, the neuron is harder to fire than it is at rest. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The neuron has run out of neurotransmitters.
The neuron is still depolarized, so it cannot depolarize again.
The myelin sheath is temporarily blocking the axon.
The membrane is more negative than its resting potential, so a stronger stimulus is needed to reach threshold.
questions.explanation: After an action potential, potassium continues to leave briefly, so the membrane overshoots to about \(-80\) mV. This refractory period limits how quickly a neuron can fire again.

questions.stem: A researcher increases the strength of the stimulus delivered to the neuron graphed. How will the neuron's response change, assuming the stimulus was already above threshold?
choices: The neuron will fire more frequently, but each action potential will reach the same peak.
Each action potential will reach a higher peak, such as \(+80\) mV.
The resting potential will become more positive.
The neuron will stop firing because it is overstimulated.
questions.explanation: Firing is all-or-none: once threshold is reached, every action potential has the same size. The nervous system signals a stronger stimulus by a higher firing rate and by recruiting more neurons.

questions.stem: A medication for depression prevents the sending neuron from reabsorbing serotonin after it is released. What is the most direct effect?
choices: The receiving neuron's serotonin receptors are blocked.
The sending neuron produces less serotonin.
Serotonin remains in the synapse longer, increasing its effect on the receiving neuron.
Serotonin is converted into dopamine in the synapse.
questions.explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block reuptake, the process by which a sending neuron reabsorbs excess neurotransmitter. More serotonin stays available to bind with receptors.

questions.stem: Curare, a plant poison, binds to acetylcholine receptors at muscles without activating them, causing paralysis. How is curare classified?
choices: As an agonist, because it mimics the neurotransmitter
As a reuptake inhibitor, because it keeps acetylcholine in the synapse
As a hormone, because it acts on muscles
As an antagonist, because it blocks the neurotransmitter's action
questions.explanation: An antagonist occupies receptor sites without triggering them, preventing the natural neurotransmitter from acting. Because acetylcholine triggers muscle contraction, blocking it causes paralysis.

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines reduce anxiety by enhancing the effect of a neurotransmitter at its receptors. Which neurotransmitter is it, and what is its main role?
choices: Glutamate, the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter
Dopamine, which is involved in reward and movement
GABA, the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are GABA agonists. Increasing inhibition calms neural activity, which reduces anxiety and can cause drowsiness. Too little GABA activity is linked to anxiety and seizures.

questions.stem: A patient develops tremors, muscle rigidity, and difficulty starting movements. Treatment with L-dopa, a precursor of a neurotransmitter, improves the symptoms. Which neurotransmitter is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: These are symptoms of Parkinson's disease, in which dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra die. L-dopa crosses into the brain and is converted to dopamine.

questions.stem: After months of drinking coffee daily, a student needs three cups to feel as alert as one cup once made them feel. Which concept does this describe?
questions.explanation: Tolerance develops as the brain adapts to repeated drug use, so a larger dose is needed for the same effect. Withdrawal refers to the unpleasant symptoms, such as headaches, that occur when the drug is stopped.

questions.stem: A drug increases heart rate, alertness, and feelings of euphoria for several hours, after which the user feels fatigued and depressed. To which class of drugs does it most likely belong?
questions.explanation: Stimulants, such as cocaine and amphetamines, speed up nervous system activity, often by increasing dopamine and norepinephrine. The later crash reflects the brain's depleted neurotransmitter supply.

questions.stem: After damage to the region labeled A, a once-careful accountant becomes impulsive, makes poor decisions, and struggles to plan ahead. Which lobe was most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: Region A is the frontal lobe, whose prefrontal cortex supports planning, judgment, and impulse control. Phineas Gage's personality changes after his injury are the classic example.

questions.stem: A stroke damages the region labeled C, while the eyes remain healthy. Which difficulty is the patient most likely to have?
choices: Loss of the sense of touch on one side of the body
Problems seeing or recognizing objects in part of the visual field
questions.explanation: Region C is the occipital lobe, which contains the primary visual cortex. Damage there can cause blindness in part of the visual field even though the eyes work normally.

questions.stem: A patient speaks fluently, but the speech makes little sense, and the patient has great difficulty understanding what others say. Damage to the left side of which region is most likely?
questions.explanation: These symptoms describe Wernicke's aphasia. Wernicke's area, which supports language comprehension, lies in the left temporal lobe near the auditory cortex.

questions.explanation: Region B is the parietal lobe. The somatosensory cortex lies just behind the central groove that separates it from the frontal lobe, where the motor cortex lies.

questions.stem: A police officer asks a driver to walk heel-to-toe in a straight line. This test checks for impaired functioning of which labeled structure?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates balance and smooth, precise movements. Alcohol impairs its function, so a person who is intoxicated has difficulty with tasks requiring fine motor coordination.

questions.stem: A patient understands questions well but speaks slowly in short, effortful phrases, such as "Walk… dog… park." Damage to which area is most likely?
choices: Broca's area in the left frontal lobe
Wernicke's area in the left temporal lobe
questions.explanation: Broca's area controls the muscle movements of speech. Damage produces nonfluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension, the opposite pattern from Wernicke's aphasia.

questions.stem: A split-brain patient stares at a central dot while the word "key" is flashed briefly to the left visual field. Which response is most likely?
choices: The patient says "key" aloud and picks a key with the right hand.
The patient says "key" aloud but cannot pick it out with either hand.
The patient says they saw nothing, but the left hand can pick out a key by touch.
The patient cannot respond in any way.
questions.explanation: Information from the left visual field goes to the right hemisphere, which usually cannot produce speech. With the corpus callosum cut, the information cannot reach the left hemisphere's language areas, but the right hemisphere controls the left hand.

questions.stem: After surgery that removed parts of both temporal lobes, a patient could no longer form new memories of facts and events but remembered his childhood well. Which structure was most likely removed?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is essential for forming new explicit (declarative) memories, as the case of patient H.M. showed. Older memories, already stored elsewhere in the cortex, remained.

questions.stem: Which brain structure regulates hunger, thirst, and body temperature and controls the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus maintains homeostasis through these drives and links the nervous system to the endocrine system by directing the pituitary, often called the master gland.

questions.stem: An injury to which structure is most likely to be immediately life-threatening because it controls breathing and heart rate?
questions.explanation: The medulla, in the brainstem, controls automatic survival functions such as breathing and heartbeat. Damage there can stop these functions.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has the left hemisphere removed to stop severe seizures. Over several years, the child regains much of the ability to speak. Which concept does this best illustrate?
choices: Neuroplasticity, which is greatest in childhood
Hemispheric lateralization, which prevents language from shifting
questions.explanation: The brain can reorganize by forming new connections, and this capacity is greatest early in life. Here the right hemisphere took over language functions usually handled by the left.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to know exactly when, to the millisecond, brain activity changes as a participant recognizes a face. Which method is best suited?
choices: fMRI, because it shows which areas use the most oxygen
A lesion study, because it shows which area is necessary
EEG, because it records electrical activity with very precise timing
A CT scan, because it shows brain structure
questions.explanation: An EEG measures electrical activity at the scalp with millisecond timing, though it localizes activity poorly. An fMRI shows where activity occurs more precisely but tracks blood flow, which changes over seconds.

questions.stem: After a near-collision while driving, a person's racing heart gradually slows and digestion resumes. Which division of the nervous system produces this calming?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic division prepares the body for fight or flight, while the parasympathetic division restores calm and conserves energy. Both are branches of the autonomic nervous system.

questions.stem: A traveler who flies across six time zones feels wide awake at 3 a.m. local time. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The traveler is in REM sleep while awake.
The pituitary gland has stopped releasing hormones.
The traveler's sleep debt has been fully repaid.
The traveler's circadian rhythm, regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus and the timing of melatonin release, is still set to the home time zone.
questions.explanation: Jet lag occurs because the body's roughly 24-hour clock, set by light acting on the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus, takes days to shift to a new schedule. The pineal gland releases melatonin when that clock signals night.

questions.stem: How do the REM periods in the hypnogram change over the course of the night?

They become longer and more frequent toward morning.
They occur only in the first cycle.

questions.stem: A child often sleepwalks but has no memory of it the next morning. Based on the hypnogram, when during the night is sleepwalking most likely to occur?
choices: In the last few hours, during REM sleep
At random times, because it is unrelated to sleep stages
In the first few hours, during N3 sleep
questions.explanation: Sleepwalking and night terrors occur during deep N3 sleep, which is concentrated early in the night. In REM sleep, the body's major muscles are largely paralyzed, which normally prevents acting out dreams.

questions.stem: During the day, a person suddenly falls asleep while talking and briefly enters REM sleep, sometimes losing muscle tone after laughing. Which sleep disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: Narcolepsy involves uncontrollable sleep attacks that can lead directly into REM sleep. Cataplexy, the sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, is a hallmark of the disorder.

figure.alt: Table of concordance rates for a hypothetical disorder X. Identical twins raised together: 100 percent of genes shared, 48 percent concordance. Identical twins raised apart: 100 percent, 44 percent. Fraternal twins raised together: 50 percent, 17 percent. Non-twin siblings: 50 percent, 9 percent. Unrelated children raised together: about 0 percent, 2 percent

questions.stem: Which comparison in the table provides the strongest evidence that genes contribute to disorder X?
choices: Fraternal twins have a higher concordance than non-twin siblings.
Unrelated children raised together have a low concordance.
Identical twins raised apart have a much higher concordance than fraternal twins raised together.
Non-twin siblings have a concordance of 9 percent.
questions.explanation: Identical twins raised apart share all of their genes but not their environment, yet their concordance is far higher than that of fraternal twins, who share an environment and half of their genes. This pattern points to a genetic influence.

figure.alt: Table of concordance rates for a hypothetical disorder X. Identical twins raised together: 100 percent of genes shared, 48 percent concordance. Identical twins raised apart: 100 percent, 44 percent. Fraternal twins raised together: 50 percent, 17 percent. Non-twin siblings: 50 percent, 9 percent. Unrelated children raised together: about 0 percent, 2 percent

questions.stem: Which conclusion about disorder X is best supported by the fact that concordance for identical twins is well below 100 percent?
choices: The disorder is caused entirely by genes.
Identical twins do not actually share all of their genes.
The disorder cannot be studied with twin research.
Environmental factors also influence whether a person develops the disorder.
questions.explanation: If genes alone determined the disorder, an identical twin of someone affected would always be affected as well. A concordance near 48 percent indicates that nongenetic factors, such as experiences, also play a role.

figure.alt: Graph of the percentage of trials on which a participant detected a faint light at different intensities. Detection rises in an S-shaped curve from near 0 percent at intensity 1 to near 100 percent at intensity 9, crossing 50 percent at intensity 5, marked with dashed lines

questions.stem: Based on the graph, what is the participant's absolute threshold for the light?
choices: An intensity of 1, the lowest intensity ever detected
An intensity of 9, detected on nearly all trials
An intensity of 5, detected on 50 percent of trials
An intensity of 10, the strongest stimulus tested
questions.explanation: The absolute threshold is defined as the minimum stimulus intensity detected 50 percent of the time. Detection does not jump from 0 to 100 percent, so a single cutoff would not describe the data.

questions.stem: For a certain participant, the just noticeable difference for weight is 2 percent. If the participant holds a 400-gram object, how much weight must be added before they notice a difference?
questions.explanation: Weber's law states that the just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus. Two percent of 400 grams is 8 grams; for a 100-gram object, 2 grams would suffice.

figure.alt: Table of results for two radiologists who each examined 100 scans, 50 with a tumor and 50 without. Radiologist P: 47 hits, 3 misses, 28 false alarms, and 22 correct rejections. Radiologist Q: 31 hits, 19 misses, 4 false alarms, and 46 correct rejections

questions.stem: Two radiologists each examined the same 100 scans. Which statement best describes radiologist P compared with radiologist Q?
choices: P uses a more liberal response criterion, saying "tumor present" more readily, which produces more hits but also more false alarms.
P has better eyesight, so P detects more tumors without any cost.
P uses a more conservative criterion, which reduces false alarms.
P and Q differ only by chance, because both examined 100 scans.
questions.explanation: Signal detection theory separates sensitivity from response bias. P says "tumor" far more often, catching nearly every tumor but also flagging 28 healthy scans. Expectations and the costs of a miss can shift a person's criterion in this way.

questions.stem: A person who enters a bakery notices the strong smell of bread, but after twenty minutes no longer notices it. Which concept explains this?
choices: Transduction, the conversion of stimulus energy into neural signals
Signal detection, the decision about whether a stimulus is present
Sensory adaptation, a decrease in sensitivity to an unchanging stimulus
Selective attention, the choice to focus on a different stimulus
questions.explanation: Sensory receptors respond less to constant stimulation, which frees attention for changes in the environment. The smell is still present, but the person's sensory response to it has decreased.

questions.stem: After staring at a solid green square for a minute, a person looks at a white wall and sees a red square. Which theory best explains this?
questions.explanation: Opponent-process theory proposes that color is processed in pairs, such as red–green. Prolonged green stimulation fatigues the green response, so the paired red response dominates when the eyes view white.

questions.stem: On a dark night, a star is easier to see by looking slightly to the side of it rather than directly at it. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Cones, which are concentrated in the periphery, detect dim light.
The fovea contains only rods, which see color.
Looking to the side reduces sensory adaptation in the optic nerve.
Rods, which are concentrated in the periphery of the retina, are more sensitive to dim light than cones.
questions.explanation: The fovea, at the center of the retina, contains mostly cones, which need bright light and detect color and detail. Rods outside the fovea respond to very dim light.

questions.stem: After years of exposure to loud music, a guitarist has permanent hearing loss caused by damage to the hair cells of the cochlea. What type of hearing loss is this?
choices: Hearing loss caused by damage to the eardrum
questions.explanation: Sensorineural hearing loss results from damage to the cochlea's receptor cells or the auditory nerve and is usually permanent. Conduction hearing loss involves the eardrum or middle-ear bones, which carry vibrations to the cochlea.

questions.stem: Most people describe the pattern of dots shown as four vertical stripes, or pairs of columns, rather than six rows. Which Gestalt principle explains this?
questions.explanation: The principle of proximity states that elements close together are grouped. All of the dots look alike, so the grouping comes only from the narrow and wide gaps between columns.

questions.stem: The two lines in the figure are the same length, but most viewers judge line B to be longer. Studies have found that the illusion is weaker among people raised in environments with few rectangular buildings. What does this finding suggest?
choices: The illusion is caused by a defect in the retina.
People from such environments have better eyesight.
Perception is determined entirely by the physical stimulus.
Experience with corners and depth cues shapes how people interpret the figure.
questions.explanation: One explanation is that the fins resemble the corners of rooms and buildings, which serve as depth cues. People with more experience of such "carpentered" environments may interpret the figure in depth, showing that perception depends partly on learning.

questions.stem: A person easily reads the sentence "Tihs snetence is esay to raed" even though the words are misspelled. Which concept best explains this?
choices: Top-down processing, in which knowledge and expectations guide perception
Bottom-up processing, which builds perception from individual features
questions.explanation: The reader's knowledge of words and context fills in what the jumbled letters only partly provide. Bottom-up processing would analyze each letter as it appears.

questions.stem: Participants who are first shown several pictures of animals are more likely to see an ambiguous sketch as a rat, while those first shown faces see it as a man's face. What does this demonstrate?
choices: Perceptual constancy, which keeps perception stable as conditions change
Perceptual set, a mental predisposition to perceive one thing rather than another
questions.explanation: Recent experiences create expectations that influence how ambiguous stimuli are interpreted. This is a form of top-down processing.

questions.stem: A person who has lost the sight of one eye can still judge that a car far down the road is distant because it appears small and is partly hidden by a tree. Which kind of cues is the person using?
choices: Binocular cues, such as retinal disparity
Monocular cues, such as relative size and interposition
questions.explanation: Monocular cues require only one eye. Retinal disparity and convergence, which compare information from the two eyes, are binocular cues that this person can no longer use.

questions.stem: As a door swings open, the image it casts on the retina changes from a rectangle to a narrow trapezoid, yet the observer still perceives a rectangular door. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Perceptual constancy allows people to perceive objects as unchanging even as their retinal images change. Shape constancy keeps the door looking rectangular as its angle changes.

questions.stem: Participants counting basketball passes in a video often fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. Which concept does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: When attention is focused on one task, people can fail to see an unexpected but clearly visible object. Change blindness, by contrast, is failing to notice that something has changed between views.

questions.stem: During a conversation, a stranger asking for directions is replaced by a different person while a door is carried between them. Many participants do not notice the switch. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Change blindness is the failure to detect changes in a scene, especially across a brief interruption. People store far less visual detail than they believe they do.

questions.stem: When asked to think of a bird, most people imagine a robin rather than a penguin, and they decide more quickly that a robin is a bird. Which concept explains this?
choices: A prototype, the best example of a category
questions.explanation: People categorize by comparing new items with a prototype. The closer an item is to the prototype, the more quickly it is identified as a member of the category.

questions.stem: To find a misplaced key, a person searches every room in the house systematically, one drawer at a time. Which problem-solving strategy is this?
choices: An algorithm, which guarantees a solution but can be slow
Trial and error guided by intuition
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a methodical procedure that guarantees a solution if one exists. A heuristic, such as checking the places the key is usually left, is faster but can fail.

questions.stem: After watching news coverage of a plane crash, a traveler decides to drive across the country instead of flying, though driving is statistically far more dangerous. Which concept best explains the decision?
questions.explanation: The availability heuristic judges likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent images of a crash make flying seem riskier than it is.

questions.stem: Told that a person is quiet, loves poetry, and wears glasses, most people guess the person is a literature professor rather than a truck driver, though truck drivers are far more numerous. Which concept is illustrated?
questions.explanation: The representativeness heuristic judges by how well something matches a prototype, while ignoring base rates. Because many more people drive trucks, the odds favor a truck driver despite the description.

questions.stem: Given a candle, a box of tacks, and matches, and asked to attach the candle to a wall, many people fail to think of emptying the box and tacking it up as a shelf. Which barrier to problem solving does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Functional fixedness is the tendency to see objects only in their usual roles. Seeing the box only as a container blocks the solution.

questions.stem: A student who believes a lucky shirt improves test scores remembers every good score earned while wearing it but overlooks the bad ones. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek and remember evidence that supports existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence.

questions.stem: Patients are more likely to choose a surgery described as having a "90 percent survival rate" than one described as having a "10 percent mortality rate." Which concept does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: The two descriptions present identical information. The framing effect shows that the way a choice is worded can change decisions.

questions.stem: After a roulette wheel lands on red seven times in a row, a gambler bets heavily on black, believing it is "due." Which error is this?
questions.explanation: Each spin is independent, so the chance of black is the same as on every other spin. The gambler's fallacy is the belief that past random events change future probabilities.

questions.stem: A test designed to predict how well students will learn in a future course, rather than to measure what they have already learned, is best described as which kind of test?
questions.explanation: Aptitude tests predict future performance or ability to learn, while achievement tests measure what a person has already learned, such as a final exam.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the high recall of the first few words in the graph?
choices: The early words were still in short-term memory at the time of recall.
The early words were more meaningful than the others.
The early words were rehearsed more and transferred into long-term memory.
The participants guessed the early words.
questions.explanation: This is the primacy effect. Early items receive more rehearsal before new words compete for attention. The recency effect, for the last words, reflects items still held in short-term memory.

questions.stem: The researchers repeat the study but have participants count backward for 30 seconds before recalling the list. How would the graph most likely change?
choices: Recall of the first few words would drop, while recall of the last few would stay high.
Recall of the last few words would drop, while recall of the first few would stay high.
Recall of every word would increase.
The curve would stay the same.
questions.explanation: Counting backward displaces items held in short-term memory, which eliminates the recency effect. Words already transferred to long-term memory, producing the primacy effect, are unaffected.

questions.stem: A person can remember the letters "FBICIANASA" by grouping them as FBI, CIA, and NASA. Which strategy is this?
choices: Chunking, which increases the amount of information held in short-term memory
Maintenance rehearsal, which transfers information into sensory memory
questions.explanation: Short-term memory holds roughly seven items. Chunking groups items into meaningful units, so ten letters become three chunks.

questions.stem: Participants find it much harder to remember a list of words while repeating "the, the, the" aloud than while tapping a pattern with their fingers. Which part of working memory does repeating a word most interfere with?
questions.explanation: Baddeley's model includes a phonological loop for verbal and sound-based information and a visuospatial sketchpad for images. Repeating a word occupies the phonological loop, which is also needed to rehearse the list.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about encoding is best supported by the graph?
choices: Processing words for meaning produces better recall than processing them for their appearance or sound.
Rhyming is the most effective way to remember words.
The font of a word has no effect on whether it is recalled.
Participants recalled the same number of words in each condition.
questions.explanation: Recall rose from 18 to 68 percent as processing became deeper. The levels-of-processing model proposes that deeper, semantic encoding produces more durable memories.

questions.stem: In the study shown, what is the independent variable?
choices: The number of words in the list
The kind of question participants answered about each word
questions.explanation: The researchers manipulated the kind of question, which determined the depth of processing. The percentage recalled is the dependent variable, the outcome measured.

questions.stem: Two students study for the same number of total hours. One studies in six short sessions over two weeks, and the other in one long session the night before. Which result is most likely?
choices: The second student remembers more, because of the recency effect.
The first student remembers more, because of the spacing effect.
Both remember the same amount, because study time is equal.
The second student remembers more, because massed practice reduces interference.
questions.explanation: Distributed practice produces better long-term retention than massed practice, or cramming. Spaced sessions give repeated opportunities to retrieve and consolidate the material.

questions.stem: To memorize a speech, a student imagines placing each main point in a different room of their house and then mentally walks through the house. Which strategy is this?
questions.explanation: The method of loci links each item to a familiar location, using vivid imagery and a fixed order to aid retrieval.

questions.stem: A patient with amnesia cannot remember practicing a new skill, such as tracing a star while looking in a mirror, yet improves at the task each day. What does this show?
choices: Explicit memory is needed to learn any skill.
Semantic memory is stored in the hippocampus.
Implicit procedural memory can form even when explicit memory is impaired.
questions.explanation: Procedural memories, such as skills, are implicit and depend on structures such as the cerebellum and basal ganglia, not the hippocampus. Patients like H.M. showed this dissociation.

questions.stem: A student remembers that the capital of France is Paris and also remembers a family trip to Paris last summer. How are these memories classified?
choices: The first is semantic memory, and the second is episodic memory.
The first is episodic memory, and the second is semantic memory.
questions.explanation: Both are explicit memories. Semantic memory holds general facts and knowledge, while episodic memory holds personally experienced events tied to a time and place.

choices: Learning on land always produces better recall.
Recall was better when the testing environment matched the learning environment.
The testing location had no effect on recall.
questions.explanation: Divers recalled 14 and 12 words when the places matched, and only 9 when they did not. Context-dependent memory occurs because cues present during encoding help retrieval.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the pattern in the graph?
choices: Divers who learned on land recalled fewer words in both locations.
Testing underwater lowered recall for both groups.
The groups' recall differed by the same amount in both locations.
The effect of the testing location depended on where the words were learned.
questions.explanation: The bars cross over: land testing helped the land group, while underwater testing helped the underwater group. When the effect of one variable depends on another, the variables interact.

questions.stem: A person who is sad finds it easier to recall other sad times in their life. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Mood-congruent memory is the tendency to recall experiences consistent with one's current mood. A sad mood primes sad associations, which can reinforce depression.

questions.stem: Students often find multiple-choice questions easier than fill-in-the-blank questions on the same material. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Recognition requires identifying information that is presented, which is easier than recall.
Recognition requires more retrieval cues to be generated by the learner.
questions.explanation: Recall requires retrieving information with few cues, while recognition provides the information to be identified. People can often recognize far more than they can recall.

figure.alt: Graph of the percentage of learned nonsense syllables retained over six days. Retention drops steeply within the first day, from 100 percent to about 33 percent, and then levels off near 22 percent for the remaining days

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the pattern of forgetting in the graph?
choices: Most forgetting occurs soon after learning, and the rate of forgetting then slows.
Forgetting occurs at a steady rate over the six days.
Little is forgotten during the first day.
All of the material is forgotten within six days.
questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus found that retention drops steeply within hours and then levels off. The material still retained after several days is relatively stable.

figure.alt: Graph of the percentage of learned nonsense syllables retained over six days. Retention drops steeply within the first day, from 100 percent to about 33 percent, and then levels off near 22 percent for the remaining days

questions.stem: Ebbinghaus found that even when he could not recall a list, he relearned it faster than he had learned it the first time. What does this show?
choices: Relearning is a measure of short-term memory.
The list had been completely forgotten.
Some memory remained, as measured by relearning, even when recall failed.
Recall is a more sensitive measure of memory than relearning.
questions.explanation: The time saved in relearning reveals retained memory that recall tests miss. Relearning is the most sensitive of the three measures: recall, recognition, and relearning.

questions.stem: After moving, a person keeps typing the old address when filling out forms. What explains the difficulty in remembering the new address?
questions.explanation: In proactive interference, older information disrupts the recall of newer information. In retroactive interference, new learning disrupts the recall of older information.

questions.stem: Participants who watched a video of a car crash estimated higher speeds and were more likely to "remember" broken glass when asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed" rather than "hit." Which concept does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Loftus and Palmer showed that misleading wording after an event can alter memories of it. Memory is reconstructive rather than an exact record.

figure.alt: A normal distribution of IQ scores with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. The axis is marked at 55, 70, 85, 100, 115, 130, and 145. The region between 85 and 115 is shaded

questions.stem: On an IQ test with the distribution shown, about what percentage of people score in the shaded region, between 85 and 115?
questions.explanation: In a normal distribution, about 68 percent of scores fall within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent within two, and about 99.7 percent within three.

figure.alt: A normal distribution of IQ scores with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. The axis is marked at 55, 70, 85, 100, 115, 130, and 145. The region between 85 and 115 is shaded

questions.stem: About what percentage of test takers score above 130 on the test whose distribution is shown?
questions.explanation: A score of 130 is two standard deviations above the mean. About 95 percent of scores lie within two standard deviations, so about 2.5 percent lie above 130; a score of 130 is near the 98th percentile.

questions.stem: Which property of the new test does the scatterplot best demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Reliability is the consistency of a measure. The points cluster tightly around a line, showing a strong positive correlation between scores on two occasions. The graph says nothing about whether the test measures what it claims to.

questions.stem: A new test gives each person nearly the same score every time it is taken, but scores do not correlate with students' grades or any other measure of the ability it claims to assess. How is the test best described?
questions.explanation: Consistent scores show reliability. Validity is whether a test measures or predicts what it is supposed to. A test can be reliable without being valid, but a test with poor reliability cannot be valid.

questions.stem: Women who are told before a difficult math test that men usually outperform women score lower than women who are told the test shows no gender differences. Which concept does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Stereotype threat is a concern that one will confirm a negative stereotype about one's group. The anxiety and distraction it causes can reduce performance, which may contribute to group differences in test scores.

questions.stem: To study how memory changes with age, a researcher tests 20-, 40-, 60-, and 80-year-olds at the same time. Which limitation is most important for this design?
choices: The study will take many decades to complete.
Participants are likely to drop out over time.
The same participants will become familiar with the test.
Differences may reflect the different experiences of each generation rather than aging itself.
questions.explanation: This is a cross-sectional study. Its groups differ in birth cohort as well as age, so cohort effects, such as differences in education, can be mistaken for effects of aging. Longitudinal studies, which follow the same people, avoid this problem but take years.

questions.stem: A child born to a mother who drank heavily during pregnancy has a small head, distinctive facial features, and intellectual disability. What best describes the cause?
choices: The child inherited a dominant gene for the condition.
The child experienced too little stimulation after birth.
Alcohol acted as a teratogen, harming prenatal development.
The child's brain was overly pruned during adolescence.
questions.explanation: Teratogens are agents, such as alcohol, some drugs, and viruses, that harm the developing embryo or fetus. These symptoms describe fetal alcohol syndrome.

questions.stem: Ducklings follow the first moving object they see within a day or two of hatching, even a person, and they do not form this attachment if the window passes. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: A critical period is a limited window in which certain experiences must occur for normal development. Lorenz showed that geese and ducks imprint on a moving object during a brief window after hatching.

questions.stem: When a newborn's cheek is stroked, the baby turns toward the touch and opens its mouth. What is this response called?
questions.explanation: The rooting reflex helps a newborn find a nipple to feed. Like other newborn reflexes, it is an inborn, automatic response that fades in the first months.

choices: The infants could not distinguish the faces.
The infants were tired by trial 7.
The infants could tell the new face from the old one.
questions.explanation: Looking time falls as the infants habituate to the repeated face. Renewed interest when the new face appears, called dishabituation, shows that they perceived it as different.

questions.stem: In the study shown, what is the dependent variable?
choices: The time the infants spent looking at the display
Whether the face shown was new or familiar
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what the researchers measure: looking time. Whether the face was familiar or new is the variable the researchers manipulated.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why adolescents are, on average, more likely than adults to take risks, especially with peers present?
choices: The adolescent brain has stopped forming new synapses.
Adolescents have fewer dopamine receptors than adults.
The prefrontal cortex, which supports judgment and impulse control, matures later than reward-related areas of the brain.
questions.explanation: The limbic reward system matures earlier than the prefrontal cortex, which continues to develop into the mid-20s. This imbalance can make rewards, including peer approval, especially compelling.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary sex characteristic that develops during puberty?
questions.explanation: Primary sex characteristics are the reproductive organs and external genitalia. Secondary sex characteristics, such as facial hair, voice changes, and body shape, are other traits that develop during puberty.

questions.stem: Which change in cognitive abilities is most typical from middle adulthood to late adulthood?
choices: Fluid intelligence grows, while crystallized intelligence declines.
Crystallized intelligence remains stable or grows, while fluid intelligence declines.
questions.explanation: Accumulated knowledge and vocabulary, crystallized intelligence, tend to hold steady or increase. Speed of processing and solving novel problems, fluid intelligence, gradually decline.

questions.stem: A young child insists that only girls can be nurses and organizes toys into "boy toys" and "girl toys." Which concept best explains this behavior?
choices: Gender identity, the sense of being male, female, or another gender
Gender schemas, mental frameworks for organizing information about gender
questions.explanation: Gender schema theory proposes that children learn their culture's concepts of gender and use them to organize perceptions and behavior. Gender identity, by contrast, is a person's own internal sense of their gender.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old stops looking for a toy as soon as it is covered by a blanket, while a 10-month-old lifts the blanket to find it. What has the older infant developed?
choices: Object permanence, in the sensorimotor stage
Abstract reasoning, in the formal operational stage
Theory of mind, in the concrete operational stage
questions.explanation: Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight. Piaget believed it develops by about 8 months, though later research suggests it begins earlier.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old watches juice poured from glass A into glass B and then says glass B has more juice. Which statement best explains the child's answer?
choices: The child is in the sensorimotor stage and lacks object permanence.
The child is in the formal operational stage and is reasoning hypothetically.
The child is in the preoperational stage and has not yet mastered conservation.
The child is showing egocentrism by refusing to agree.
questions.explanation: Preoperational children focus on one dimension, here the height of the juice, and do not yet understand that quantity stays the same when its shape changes.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old watches the same demonstration and says the glasses hold the same amount. Which explanation would the child most likely give?
choices: "Glass B is taller, so it has more."
"Glass A is wider, so it has more."
"I don't know, because I can't see the juice anymore."
"If you poured it back, it would look the same as before."
questions.explanation: Concrete operational children understand reversibility: an action can be mentally undone. They also consider height and width together rather than one dimension at a time.

questions.stem: A teenager argues about what society might be like if money had never been invented, reasoning systematically about possibilities that do not exist. Which stage does this reflect?
questions.explanation: Formal operational thinking, beginning around adolescence, allows abstract and hypothetical reasoning. Concrete operational thinkers reason logically mainly about concrete events.

questions.stem: A toddler who knows the word "dog" calls a cat "doggy." Later, after being corrected, the child forms a new category for cats. Which processes are shown, in order?
questions.explanation: In assimilation, new experiences are fit into an existing schema. In accommodation, the schema is changed or a new one is created to fit the new information.

questions.stem: A parent helps a child complete a puzzle the child cannot do alone by giving hints and gradually withdrawing help as the child improves. Which concept does this describe?
choices: Scaffolding within the zone of proximal development
Conservation within the concrete operational stage
questions.explanation: Vygotsky described the zone of proximal development as the range of tasks a child can do with help but not alone. Scaffolding is temporary support that is reduced as competence grows.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old watches a puppet hide a marble in a basket and leave. Another puppet moves the marble to a box. Asked where the first puppet will look, the child points to the box. What does this suggest?
choices: The child has not yet developed a theory of mind.
The child is in the formal operational stage.
questions.explanation: Understanding that others can hold false beliefs is part of theory of mind, which usually develops around age 4 or 5. The child assumes the puppet knows what the child knows.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old says, "I goed to the store and saw two mouses." What do these errors show?
choices: The child is applying grammatical rules to words that are exceptions, called overgeneralization.
The child is in the babbling stage.
The child has not learned any grammar.
The child is imitating adult speech exactly.
questions.explanation: Adults do not say "goed," so the errors show that children actively learn rules, here for past tenses and plurals, rather than only imitating. They later learn the irregular exceptions.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old says, "Want juice" and "Daddy go." Which stage of language development does this represent?
questions.explanation: In telegraphic speech, children combine mainly nouns and verbs in short, sensible phrases while omitting small function words, like a telegram.

questions.stem: How many morphemes are in the word "unhappiness"?
questions.explanation: A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning. "Unhappiness" contains "un-" (not), "happy," and "-ness" (a state of). Phonemes, by contrast, are the smallest units of sound.

questions.explanation: Infant 3 is intensely upset by separation and both seeks and resists contact on reunion. This pattern has been linked to caregivers who respond inconsistently. Infant 4's confused, contradictory behavior is the disorganized pattern.

questions.stem: In Harlow's studies, infant monkeys spent most of their time clinging to a soft cloth "mother" rather than a wire "mother" that provided milk. What did this show?
choices: Attachment depends mainly on which caregiver provides food.
Monkeys do not form attachments to caregivers.
Contact comfort is more important than feeding in forming attachment.
Attachment forms only during a critical period of a few hours.
questions.explanation: The finding contradicted the view that infants become attached to the person who feeds them. Comforting physical contact proved central to attachment.

questions.stem: A parent sets clear rules and high expectations but explains the reasons for them and listens to the child's views. Which parenting style is this, and what outcomes is it most associated with?
choices: Authoritative; higher self-esteem and social competence
questions.explanation: Baumrind's research links the authoritative style, which combines warmth with firm limits, to positive outcomes. These are correlational findings, so other factors may also contribute.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old looks back on life with satisfaction, feeling it was meaningful despite some regrets. According to Erikson, which stage has this person resolved successfully?
questions.explanation: Erikson's final stage, in late adulthood, involves reflecting on one's life. Success brings a sense of integrity, while failure brings despair and regret.

questions.stem: A child receives a painful shot from a nurse in a white coat. Afterward, the child cries whenever anyone in a white coat approaches. In this example, what is the white coat?
questions.explanation: The shot is the unconditioned stimulus, which naturally causes fear and crying. The white coat, once neutral, was paired with the shot and now triggers the conditioned response.

questions.stem: Which phases of classical conditioning are labeled A, B, and C in the graph?
questions.explanation: In A, pairing the conditioned and unconditioned stimuli builds the response. In B, the conditioned stimulus is presented alone and the response fades. In C, the response reappears after a rest.

questions.stem: What does the segment labeled C suggest about extinction?
choices: Extinction permanently erases the conditioned response.
The unconditioned stimulus was presented again during the rest.
Extinction suppresses the conditioned response but does not completely erase the learning.
The animal learned a completely new response during the rest.
questions.explanation: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished response after a pause. Because the response returns without new pairings, the original learning must have persisted.

questions.stem: The researcher next presents the 1000 Hz tone with food and the 800 Hz and 1200 Hz tones without food. If the graph is redrawn after this training, how would it most likely change?
choices: All of the bars would become equal.
The bar for 1000 Hz would shrink.
The bars for 600 Hz and 1400 Hz would grow.
The bars for 800 Hz and 1200 Hz would shrink, while the bar for 1000 Hz would stay high.
questions.explanation: This is discrimination training. When only the 1000 Hz tone predicts food, the animal learns to distinguish it from similar tones, so its gradient becomes narrower.

questions.stem: After eating a new food and becoming sick hours later from an unrelated virus, a person develops a lasting dislike of that food after just one experience. Why is this finding significant?
choices: It shows that classical conditioning requires many pairings.
It shows that biological preparedness allows some associations to form after one pairing despite a long delay.
It shows that the conditioned and unconditioned stimuli must occur within seconds.
It shows that taste aversions are learned through operant conditioning.
questions.explanation: Garcia's research on taste aversion challenged the view that any stimulus could be paired equally well with any response. Animals are biologically prepared to link tastes with illness.

questions.stem: A car makes an annoying beeping sound until the driver fastens the seat belt. Fastening the seat belt becomes more likely in the future. Which process is this?
questions.explanation: The behavior removes an unpleasant stimulus, so it is reinforced. "Negative" means something is taken away, and reinforcement always increases a behavior.

questions.stem: A teenager who breaks curfew has their phone taken away for a week, and breaking curfew becomes less frequent. Which process is this?
questions.explanation: Removing a desired stimulus to decrease a behavior is negative punishment. Positive punishment adds an unpleasant stimulus, such as extra chores.

questions.stem: Line Y shows a scalloped pattern, with little responding just after reinforcement and rapid responding as the next one approaches. Which schedule produces this pattern?
questions.explanation: On a fixed-interval schedule, the first response after a set time is reinforced. Subjects learn that early responses do not pay off, so responding accelerates as the time nears, as when students study more just before scheduled exams.

questions.stem: To teach a dog to ring a bell, a trainer first rewards the dog for approaching the bell, then for touching it, and finally only for ringing it. What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Shaping reinforces behaviors that come closer and closer to the desired behavior. It allows behaviors that would rarely occur on their own to be trained.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about observational learning is best supported by the graph?
choices: Children who saw the model punished never learned the aggressive acts.
Rewards made the children more aggressive than the model.
Children learned the aggressive acts by observation even when they did not perform them, because they imitated them once offered a reward.
Observing a model has no effect on children's behavior.
questions.explanation: Children who saw the model punished imitated few acts, but when offered a reward they reproduced nearly as many as the others. Bandura concluded that learning had occurred; vicarious punishment suppressed only the performance.

questions.stem: Rats that explored a maze for ten days without reward suddenly ran it as fast as consistently rewarded rats once food was placed at the end. What does this demonstrate?
choices: Latent learning, which is shown only when there is an incentive
questions.explanation: Tolman concluded that the unrewarded rats had formed a cognitive map of the maze. Their learning stayed hidden until a reason to use it appeared.

questions.stem: Dogs that received shocks they could not escape later failed to escape shocks even when they could simply jump over a low barrier. Which concept does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Seligman found that experiencing uncontrollable bad events can lead an animal or a person to stop trying even when control becomes possible. Learned helplessness has been proposed as a model of some forms of depression.

questions.stem: When a new coworker arrives late to a meeting, Dana immediately concludes the coworker is lazy and irresponsible, without considering that traffic might have been heavy. Which concept does this illustrate?
choices: The actor–observer bias, from the actor's view
questions.explanation: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overestimate personal (dispositional) causes and underestimate situational causes when explaining others' behavior.

questions.stem: When Kai trips on the stairs, Kai blames the slippery steps; when a classmate trips on the same stairs, Kai thinks the classmate is clumsy. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: People tend to explain their own behavior by situations, which they can see, and others' behavior by dispositions. This difference in perspective is the actor–observer bias.

questions.stem: A student says an A on an exam reflects hard work and intelligence, but blames a C on unfair questions. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: The self-serving bias is the tendency to take credit for successes and blame failures on outside factors, which protects self-esteem.

questions.stem: A job seeker believes that getting hired depends mainly on preparation and effort, not luck or connections. Which concept does this describe?
questions.explanation: People with an internal locus of control believe they control their own outcomes. Those with an external locus of control attribute outcomes to luck, fate, or powerful others.

questions.stem: Students rate a classmate's face as more likable after seeing the classmate in the hallway many times, though they have never spoken. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Repeated exposure to a neutral stimulus tends to increase liking for it, even without any interaction.

questions.stem: Teachers were told, falsely, that certain randomly chosen students were about to bloom intellectually. By year's end those students showed greater gains. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Expectations can lead people to act in ways, such as giving more attention and encouragement, that make the expectations come true.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of discrimination rather than a stereotype or prejudice?
choices: A landlord refuses to rent to applicants of a particular ethnicity.
A person believes members of a group are all good at math.
A person feels uneasy around members of an unfamiliar group.
A person assumes older adults are bad with technology.
questions.explanation: Discrimination is behavior: unjustified negative action toward members of a group. A stereotype is a generalized belief, and prejudice is an attitude or feeling.

questions.stem: Members of a sports team describe themselves as varied individuals but describe fans of a rival team as "all the same." Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: People see more variety within their own group and view members of other groups as similar to one another. This tendency, along with in-group bias, can foster stereotyping.

questions.stem: In the study shown, participants performed a dull task and some were then paid to tell another person it was fun. Which group rated the task most enjoyable, and why?
choices: The $20 group, because the larger reward made the task more pleasant
The control group, because they did not have to lie
The $1 and $20 groups equally, because both were paid
The $1 group, because the small payment did not justify lying, so they changed their attitude to match what they said
questions.explanation: Festinger and Carlsmith's cognitive dissonance theory explains the result. The $20 group had ample justification for lying; the $1 group reduced the discomfort of acting against their attitude by deciding the task was enjoyable.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the $20 group's ratings were similar to the control group's ratings?
choices: The $20 group did not actually perform the task.
The $20 group was randomly assigned to enjoy the task.
The large payment provided sufficient external justification, so there was little dissonance to reduce.
Money always reduces how much people enjoy a task.
questions.explanation: Dissonance arises when behavior conflicts with attitudes and there is no adequate external reason for it. A large reward explains the behavior, so the attitude does not need to change.

questions.stem: A voter carefully compares the evidence in two candidates' policy proposals, while another votes for the candidate with the more attractive campaign ads. Which statement is correct?
choices: The first voter used the peripheral route, which relies on careful analysis.
The first voter used the central route to persuasion, which tends to produce more lasting attitude change.
Both voters used the central route.
The second voter's attitude is likely to be more lasting.
questions.explanation: The elaboration likelihood model distinguishes the central route, careful evaluation of arguments, from the peripheral route, responding to cues such as attractiveness. Centrally formed attitudes are more durable.

questions.stem: A salesperson first asks a customer to sign up for a free newsletter and later asks the same customer to buy a subscription. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Agreeing to a small request makes people more likely to agree to a larger one later, partly because they come to see themselves as the kind of person who agrees.

questions.stem: A fundraiser asks for a $500 donation, is refused, and then asks for $25, which the person gives. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Following a large request that is refused with a smaller one makes the smaller request seem reasonable and creates pressure to reciprocate the concession.

questions.stem: In Asch's study, participants judged which comparison line matched the standard after several confederates unanimously gave the wrong answer, line C. About a third of the time, participants also answered C. What best explains this?
choices: Normative social influence, the desire to be accepted and avoid disapproval
Informational social influence, because the task was very difficult
Obedience to the experimenter's direct orders
Social facilitation, because others were present
questions.explanation: The correct answer, B, was obvious, so participants were unlikely to doubt their own eyes. Many who conformed later said they went along to avoid standing out.

questions.stem: In a variation of the study shown, one confederate gives the correct answer, B, before the participant responds, while the others say C. How does conformity change?
choices: It increases, because the participant sees disagreement.
It stays the same, because the majority is still large.
It disappears only if the confederate is a friend.
It drops sharply, because the group is no longer unanimous.
questions.explanation: Asch found that a single dissenter greatly reduced conformity. Unanimity is one of the strongest factors in conformity.

questions.stem: In Milgram's obedience research, which change most reduced the percentage of participants who delivered the highest shock?
choices: Having the experimenter wear a lab coat
Placing the learner in the same room, so the participant had to press the learner's hand onto a shock plate
Conducting the study at a prestigious university
Having the experimenter give orders in person rather than by phone
questions.explanation: Obedience fell when the victim was closer and more personal. A legitimate, nearby authority figure increased obedience.

questions.stem: Students who mildly favor a policy discuss it in a group with others who share that view. Afterward, they favor it more strongly. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Discussion among like-minded people tends to strengthen their shared opinions. Groupthink, by contrast, is a desire for harmony that leads a group to make poor decisions by suppressing dissent.

questions.stem: A leadership team, wanting to keep the peace and confident in its success, dismisses warnings about a product's flaws and launches it, with disastrous results. Which concept best explains this decision?
questions.explanation: Groupthink occurs when the desire for agreement overrides realistic evaluation of alternatives. Assigning someone to argue against a plan and inviting outside experts can help prevent it.

questions.stem: An expert pianist performs better in front of an audience, while a beginner performs worse. Which concept explains both outcomes?
choices: Social facilitation, in which the presence of others strengthens dominant responses
Social loafing, in which individuals exert less effort in groups
Deindividuation, in which people lose self-awareness in groups
Groupthink, in which people value harmony over accuracy
questions.explanation: An audience increases arousal, which improves performance on well-learned tasks and impairs performance on difficult or new ones.

questions.stem: Which concept is best illustrated by the graph?
questions.explanation: Individual effort declines as group size increases, because each person's contribution is less identifiable and responsibility feels shared.

questions.stem: Fans wearing identical masks in a large crowd vandalize property in ways they would never do alone. Which concept best explains this behavior?
questions.explanation: Group situations that provide arousal and anonymity can reduce self-awareness and self-restraint, a state called deindividuation.

questions.stem: Which concept best explains the pattern in the graph?
choices: Social facilitation: the presence of others improves performance.
Groupthink: the group decided not to help.
Diffusion of responsibility: the more others who could help, the less responsible each person feels.
The just-world phenomenon: participants believed the victim deserved it.
questions.explanation: Darley and Latané's research on the bystander effect found that people are less likely to help when others are present, because responsibility seems to be shared among them.

questions.stem: In the study shown, what are the independent and dependent variables?
choices: The independent variable is whether participants sought help; the dependent variable is the number of listeners.
The independent variable is the number of other listeners participants believed were present; the dependent variable is whether they sought help.
The independent variable is the seizure; the dependent variable is the participants' anxiety.
Both variables are the number of listeners.
questions.explanation: The researchers manipulated how many others participants believed were present and measured whether, and how quickly, participants sought help.

questions.stem: At a summer camp, two rival groups of boys who had grown hostile became friendly after working together to fix the camp's broken water supply. Which concept explains the change?
choices: Superordinate goals, which require cooperation between groups
Group polarization, which strengthened their views
questions.explanation: In Sherif's Robbers Cave study, simple contact did not reduce hostility, but shared goals that neither group could achieve alone did.

questions.stem: After being criticized by a boss, an employee goes home and yells at their dog. Which defense mechanism does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Displacement redirects an impulse, here anger, from its true target to a safer one. Freud proposed defense mechanisms as unconscious ways the ego reduces anxiety.

questions.stem: A person who feels strong unacknowledged hostility toward a sibling becomes excessively and showily affectionate toward that sibling. Which defense mechanism does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: In reaction formation, the ego turns an unacceptable impulse into its opposite. The exaggerated quality of the affection is a typical sign.

questions.stem: Which criticism is most often made of projective tests such as the Rorschach inkblot test?
choices: They take too little time to administer.
They ask direct questions that people answer dishonestly.
They measure only the five broad personality traits.
They have low reliability and validity, because scoring depends heavily on the examiner's interpretation.
questions.explanation: Projective tests ask people to interpret ambiguous stimuli and are meant to reveal unconscious motives. Different examiners often score the same responses differently, and scores predict behavior poorly.

questions.stem: A therapist accepts a client fully, without judging the client's feelings or behavior, and listens empathetically. According to Carl Rogers, what is the purpose of this approach?
choices: To provide unconditional positive regard, which helps the client move toward a healthy self-concept and self-actualization
To reinforce the client's adaptive behaviors with rewards
To identify the client's dominant traits
questions.explanation: Rogers believed that genuineness, acceptance, and empathy help people develop a congruent self-concept and grow toward their potential.

questions.stem: According to the hierarchy shown, which need would someone stranded without food or water be expected to focus on first?
questions.explanation: Maslow proposed that needs at the base of the pyramid, such as hunger and thirst, must be met before people are strongly motivated by higher needs.

questions.stem: Which statement is a common criticism of the hierarchy shown?
choices: The hierarchy ignores biological needs entirely.
The hierarchy places self-actualization at the bottom.
The hierarchy was developed from controlled laboratory experiments.
People sometimes pursue higher needs, such as creative work or helping others, even when lower needs are unmet.
questions.explanation: Critics note that the order of needs is not fixed: people risk safety for principles or create art in poverty. Maslow's ideas also came from studying selected individuals rather than experiments.

questions.stem: A student's anxiety about speaking leads them to avoid class discussions, which keeps them from gaining confidence, which increases their anxiety. Which concept from Bandura best describes this pattern of mutual influence?
questions.explanation: Bandura proposed that behavior, personal factors such as thoughts and feelings, and the environment all influence one another.

questions.stem: After successfully finishing several difficult practice problems, a student feels confident they can master the next unit and works harder. Which concept does this describe?
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is a person's belief in their ability to succeed at a specific task. Past successes are one of its strongest sources, and it affects effort and persistence.

questions.stem: Based on the table, which person is most likely to experience frequent anxiety and mood swings?
choices: None, because the table does not measure emotional stability
questions.explanation: Neuroticism, the opposite of emotional stability, reflects a tendency toward anxiety, worry, and mood changes. L scores at the 96th percentile on this trait.

questions.stem: Based on the table, which person is most likely to be organized, careful, and reliable about meeting deadlines?
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness describes organization, discipline, and dependability. J is at the 94th percentile, while K, who is highly extraverted and open, is low on conscientiousness.

questions.stem: Which statistical technique did researchers use to identify the clusters of related behaviors that became the five-factor model of personality?
questions.explanation: Factor analysis identifies groups of items that correlate with one another, revealing underlying factors such as extraversion and conscientiousness.

figure.alt: Graph of performance versus arousal for two tasks. Both curves are inverted U shapes. Performance on a simple task peaks at a fairly high level of arousal, while performance on a complex task peaks at a lower level of arousal

questions.stem: Based on the graph, when would a student most likely perform best on a difficult, unfamiliar exam?
choices: At a relatively low to moderate level of arousal
At the highest possible level of arousal
At the same level of arousal that is best for a simple task
questions.explanation: The Yerkes–Dodson law states that performance is best at a moderate level of arousal, and that the best level is lower for complex tasks than for simple ones.

questions.stem: Children who loved drawing were promised a reward for drawing. Later, when no reward was offered, they drew less than children who had never been rewarded. Which concept does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Offering an external reward for an activity that is already enjoyable can reduce intrinsic motivation, as people begin to see the reward as their reason for doing it.

questions.stem: Which theory of emotion does the diagram represent?
questions.explanation: The two-factor theory holds that emotion requires both physiological arousal and a cognitive label for it. The same arousal could be labeled as fear or excitement depending on the situation.

questions.stem: A hiker sees a snake, notices their heart pounding, and then feels afraid. Which theory of emotion best fits the order of these events?
questions.explanation: The James–Lange theory proposes that emotion is the awareness of the body's physiological response. The Cannon–Bard theory proposes that the bodily response and the emotion occur at the same time and independently.

questions.stem: Participants who held a pen between their teeth, which forces a smile, rated cartoons as funnier than participants who held a pen between their lips. Which concept does this support?
questions.explanation: The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that facial expressions can influence the emotions people feel, not just express them. Some replications have found smaller effects than the original study.

questions.stem: In the graph, which phase is characterized by the body's high, sustained mobilization against a continuing stressor?
choices: The normal level before the stressor
questions.explanation: Selye's general adaptation syndrome has three phases. In the alarm reaction, the sympathetic system activates; in resistance, stress hormones keep the body mobilized; in exhaustion, the body's reserves are depleted.

questions.stem: According to the model shown, why is a person more vulnerable to illness during phase C?
choices: The person's sympathetic system has not yet activated.
The stressor has ended, so the body stops producing white blood cells.
The person's resistance is at its highest point.
Prolonged release of stress hormones depletes the body's resources and suppresses the immune system.
questions.explanation: Chronic stress keeps stress hormones such as cortisol elevated, which over time weakens the immune response and wears down the body.

questions.stem: A student who is anxious about failing a class makes a study schedule and meets with the teacher for extra help. Which kind of coping is this?
questions.explanation: Problem-focused coping attacks the stressor directly by changing the situation. Emotion-focused coping, such as seeking comfort from friends, manages the emotional reaction, which is useful when a stressor cannot be changed.

questions.stem: Research on Type A behavior has found that one component is most strongly linked to heart disease. Which component is it?
questions.explanation: Of the Type A traits, hostility and frequent anger are most consistently associated with heart disease, likely because of repeated activation of stress responses.

questions.stem: After a stressful day, a person seeks out friends and family and takes care of their children rather than fighting or fleeing. Which concept describes this response?
questions.explanation: The tend-and-befriend response describes coping with stress by nurturing others and seeking social support. It has been observed especially, but not only, in women.

There is a positive correlation between stressful events and illness, but the data alone cannot show that stress causes illness.
Stressful events and illness are unrelated.
